q: How many lines are on a music staff?
why: Five lines, four spaces. Every note on the page lives on one or the other.

q: In 4/4 time, a whole note lasts ___ beats.
why: A whole note fills the whole 4/4 bar. Hold it and count to four.

q: Which note is a half step above E?
why: There's no black key between E and F, so the very next key up is F.

q: What does a sharp sign do to a note?
why: A sharp moves the note one key up, the very next key, black or white.

q: The treble clef has another name. What is it?
why: Its curl wraps around the G line, the second line up from the bottom.

q: What comes next in the musical alphabet: E, F, G, ...?
why: The musical alphabet stops at G and starts over at A. Seven letters, on repeat forever.

q: In 4/4, how many beats does a quarter rest get?
why: Same length as a quarter note, just silent. Silence counts too.

q: True or false: forte means play loudly.
why: Forte is Italian for strong. Piano means soft, which is where the instrument got its full name, the pianoforte.

q: Which major key has no sharps and no flats?
why: C major is all white keys. The friendliest key on the piano.

q: Which symbol sends you back to play a section again?
why: Two dots next to a double bar line. It means do it again, not do it again louder.

q: How many sharps are in the key of A major?
why: A major has F♯, C♯ and G♯. Sharps always arrive in that order: F, C, G, D, A, E, B.

q: Which major key has exactly one flat in its key signature?
why: F major flats only B. The first flat is always B♭.

q: What interval is C up to G?
why: Count the letters C-D-E-F-G: five letters, seven half steps, a perfect 5th.

q: Which three notes spell a C major triad?
why: Root, major 3rd, perfect 5th. Lower the E and it goes minor; raise the G and it goes augmented.

q: In 4/4, a dotted half note lasts how many beats?
why: A dot adds half the note's value: 2 beats plus 1 beat equals 3.

q: What is the relative minor of C major?
why: Same key signature, no sharps or flats. Count from the parent key, A is the 6th degree, so its home chord is vi.

q: A cadence that goes V to I is called what?
why: V to I is the strongest ending in tonal music. It sounds like a door clicking shut.

q: The 'Amen' cadence at the end of many hymns goes from which chord to I?
why: IV to I is the plagal cadence. Softer than V to I, more of a nod than a slam.

q: What does a fermata tell you to do?
choices: Play the note short and detached
Hold the note longer than written
why: The fermata is the bird's eye over a note. Hold it until the conductor or your instructor says move on.

q: In G major, which note always gets a sharp?
why: G major's one sharp is F♯. It's the 7th degree, the note that leans up into G.

q: In a major key, the seventh chord built on the 7th degree is which quality?
why: In C it's B–D–F–A: diminished triad plus a minor 7th, so ø7. The fully diminished °7 needs A♭, which isn't in C major.

q: D Dorian uses the same notes as which major key?
why: D Dorian is C major starting on D. Same notes, new home base.

q: Counting numerals from the parent major key, what is D Dorian's home chord?
why: Numerals count from the parent key, C major, so D minor is ii. Calling it i is the classic slip.

q: What is the parent major key of C Mixolydian?
why: C is the 5th degree of F major, and Mixolydian is the mode on the 5th. So C Mixolydian has one flat: B♭.

q: Which mode is a major scale with a raised 4th degree?
why: Lydian is the mode on the 4th degree of its parent key. That raised 4th gives it the floaty, film-score sound.

q: Which interval is also called the tritone?
why: Three whole steps, six half steps. Spelled as a diminished 5th it's the same sound on the piano.

q: A deceptive cadence most often moves from V to which chord?
why: You expect I and get vi. The music fakes the ending and keeps going.

q: Sonata form's three main sections are:
why: Present the themes, take them apart, bring them home. The recap restates the themes, usually in the home key.

q: A ♭9 is a color tone that lives most naturally on which chord?
why: ♭9 is a dominant color. On a G7 it's A♭, and it adds tension that wants to resolve.

q: How many sharps are in the key of C♯ major?
why: Every note is sharped, even E♯ and B♯. Seven is the maximum a key signature holds.

q: How many keys are on a standard piano?
why: 52 white plus 36 black. Some pianos go past 88, but 88 is the standard.

q: How many black keys are on a standard 88-key piano?
why: 88 total minus 52 white keys leaves 36 black ones.

q: Two half notes add up to how many quarter notes?
why: Each half note is 2 quarter notes, so 2 + 2 = 4. That's one full bar of 4/4.

q: In 4/4 time, how many quarter-note beats are in one measure?
why: The top number is how many beats; the bottom 4 says the quarter note gets the beat.

q: How many eighth notes fit in one whole note?
why: Whole = 2 halves = 4 quarters = 8 eighths. Each step down doubles the count.

q: How many half steps are in one octave?
why: Count every key, black and white, from C to the next C: 12 half steps.

q: In 3/4 time, how many quarter notes fill one measure?
why: Three beats per bar, quarter note gets the beat. Waltz time.

q: A quarter note plus an eighth note equals how many eighth notes?
why: A quarter is two eighths. Add one more and you get three, the same as a dotted quarter.

q: True or false: a piano has more white keys than black keys.
why: 52 white, 36 black. White wins by 16.

q: At 60 BPM, how many clicks does a metronome make each second?
why: 60 beats per minute divided by 60 seconds is one click per second. A clock ticks at 60 BPM.

q: At 120 BPM, how long does one beat last?
why: 60 ÷ 120 = 0.5. Double the tempo, halve the beat.

q: How many sixteenth notes fit in one bar of 4/4?
why: Four per beat times four beats is 16. Count them: 1-e-and-a, 2-e-and-a...

q: A is tuned to 440 Hz. What is the frequency of the A one octave higher?
why: An octave is a 2:1 ratio. Double the frequency, same note name, one octave up.

q: If A4 is 440 Hz, what is A3, one octave lower?
why: Going down an octave halves the frequency: 440 ÷ 2 = 220.

q: In 6/8 time, how many eighth notes fill one bar?
why: Six eighths, usually felt as two big beats of three. Think of a jig.

q: How many half steps is it from C up to the nearest E above it?
why: C, C♯, D, D♯, E: four steps up. That's a major 3rd.

q: A perfect 5th has a 3:2 frequency ratio. What pure 5th sits above 200 Hz?
why: 200 × 3/2 = 300. Three wiggles of the top note for every two of the bottom.

q: A dotted quarter note equals how many sixteenth notes?
why: A quarter is 4 sixteenths, the dot adds half of that (2). Total 6.

q: At 90 BPM, how many seconds do three beats take?
why: One beat is 60 ÷ 90 = 2/3 second. Three of those make exactly 2 seconds.

q: What comes next around the circle of fifths: C, G, D, A, ...?
why: Each step goes up a perfect 5th and adds a sharp: E major has four sharps.

q: In 12-tone equal temperament, each half step multiplies the frequency by:
why: Twelve equal multiplications have to land exactly on 2, the octave. So each one is 2^(1/12).

q: In equal temperament with A4 = 440 Hz, the E a perfect 5th above is about:
why: 440 × 2^(7/12) ≈ 659.26. A pure 3:2 fifth would be 660, so the tempered fifth is a hair flat on purpose.

q: With A4 = 440 Hz in equal temperament, Middle C is about:
why: Middle C is 9 half steps below A: 440 × 2^(−9/12) ≈ 261.63 Hz.

q: To count 3 against 2 evenly, how many equal pulses do you need per cycle?
why: The least common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6. The 3 lands on pulses 1, 3, 5; the 2 lands on 1 and 4.

q: For a 4-against-3 polyrhythm, how many equal pulses make one full cycle?
why: LCM of 4 and 3 is 12. Four notes every 3 pulses against three notes every 4 pulses.

q: At 80 BPM, how many seconds does one bar of 4/4 last?
why: One beat is 60 ÷ 80 = 0.75 s. Four beats: 3 seconds flat.

q: A song in 4/4 runs 64 bars at 120 BPM. How long is it?
why: 64 bars × 4 beats = 256 beats, each 0.5 s, so 128 s, which is 2 minutes 8 seconds.

q: How many half steps are in a major 10th?
why: A major 10th is an octave (12) plus a major 3rd (4): 16 half steps.

q: The lowest A on a piano is 27.5 Hz. How many octaves up is A440?
why: 27.5 doubled four times: 55, 110, 220, 440.

q: Stack 12 pure 3:2 fifths and compare with 7 octaves. The fifths overshoot by about what ratio?
why: (3/2)^12 ÷ 2^7 ≈ 1.0136, the Pythagorean comma, about a quarter of a half step. Equal temperament spreads that error out.

q: Can sound travel through the empty vacuum of outer space?
choices: No, there's nothing to carry it
why: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle. Space is nearly empty, so astronauts talk by radio.

q: What unit do we use to measure how intense a sound is?
why: Sound intensity is measured in decibels, written dB.

q: True or false: sound travels faster in water than in air.
why: About 1,480 m/s in water versus about 343 m/s in air: more than four times faster.

q: Which snail-shaped part of the inner ear turns vibrations into nerve signals?
why: Fluid in the cochlea ripples, tiny hair cells ride the wave, and they fire signals to the brain.

q: In humpback whales, who sings the long, complex songs?
why: All humpbacks make sounds, but scientists believe only males sing the songs.

q: As an ambulance races toward you, its siren sounds:
why: That's the Doppler effect. Coming at you, the waves bunch up and the pitch goes up; driving away, it drops.

q: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
why: The stapes, in the middle ear, is about 3 mm long. It passes vibrations into the inner ear.

q: The three tiny middle-ear bones are nicknamed the hammer, the anvil, and the ___.
why: Malleus, incus, stapes: hammer, anvil, stirrup. A blacksmith's shop in your head.

q: Bats hunt in the dark with echolocation calls that are mostly too ___ for people to hear.
why: Most bat calls are ultrasound, above about 20,000 Hz. Some reach past 100,000 Hz.

q: A singer holds a note that matches a wine glass's natural pitch and the glass shakes hard. What is that called?
why: Push something at its natural frequency and each push adds to the last. Enough of that and a glass can crack.

q: About how fast does sound travel in air at 20 °C (68 °F)?
why: Roughly 343 m/s, about 767 mph. Light beats it by about a million times, which is why you see lightning first.

q: What is the commonly stated hearing range of a healthy young person?
why: 20 to 20,000 Hz, and the top end drops with age. That's normal.

q: If a sound gets 10 decibels louder, its intensity is how many times greater?
why: Decibels are logarithmic: +10 dB is 10 times the intensity, and it sounds roughly twice as loud.

q: Elephants talk with rumbles below 20 Hz, too low for us to hear. What is that range called?
why: Infrasound travels far because low frequencies lose less energy. Some elephant rumbles carry for kilometers.

q: Inside the cochlea, where are the hair cells that pick up the highest pitches?
why: High pitches are caught near the wide end, low pitches toward the center. The cochlea is a rolled-up keyboard.

q: Sprinkle sand on a vibrating metal plate and it gathers into patterns. What do the lines show?
why: Sand bounces off the moving parts and settles on the still nodal lines. These are Chladni figures, published in 1787.

q: Some people see colors when they hear music. What is this called?
why: It's a type of synesthesia. The color pairings differ from person to person but tend to stay consistent.

q: Some songbirds can sing two notes at once. Which organ lets them?
why: The syrinx has two sides with separate muscles. The Veery can sing a rising and a falling line at the same time.

q: Does sound travel faster on a hot day or a cold day?
why: Speed rises about 0.6 m/s for each degree Celsius. Warm air, faster sound.

q: Human hearing is most sensitive in which frequency range?
why: Our ears peak in the low thousands of hertz. Sounds there seem louder than equally strong bass notes.

q: Why does a clarinet jump a 12th instead of an octave when you press the register key?
choices: Its keys are made of nickel silver
Its bell is narrower than a flute's
Its reed is made of cane
It acts like a closed pipe, favoring odd harmonics
why: A closed cylinder supports odd harmonics. The 3rd harmonic is an octave plus a 5th, a 12th, so the octave gets skipped.

q: Breathe helium and your voice sounds squeaky. What actually changes?
choices: The pitch of your vocal folds
why: Sound moves faster in helium, so the throat's resonances jump up. The vocal folds vibrate at the same pitch.

q: Sound moves through steel roughly how many times faster than through air?
why: Steel carries sound around 5,900 m/s versus about 343 m/s in air. Stiffness wins.

q: In open space, each time you double your distance from a point source, the level drops about:
why: The inverse square law: the energy spreads over four times the area, which works out to about −6 dB.

q: NASA's sonification of the Perseus galaxy cluster raised its real pressure waves by about how much?
why: The black hole's note sits about 57 octaves below Middle C. The gas in the cluster carries the waves.

q: Two instruments play the same A440. What mainly makes them sound different?
choices: The size of the room only
why: Same fundamental, different recipe of overtones. That recipe is timbre.

q: Christian Doppler first proposed his effect in 1842 to explain what?
choices: The colored light of double stars
why: He was thinking about starlight. Buys Ballot tested it with sound in 1845, using a moving train.

q: Diana Deutsch's research found perfect pitch is far more common in music students who speak what?
why: In tone languages, pitch changes a word's meaning. The researchers suggest pitch learned early, like a first language, sticks.

q: True or false: in humans, cochlear hair cells killed by loud noise grow back.
why: They don't regenerate in humans, so the hearing loss is permanent.

q: The 3rd harmonic vibrates at 3 times the fundamental. How far above the fundamental does it sound?
why: Ratio 3:1 is 2:1 (octave) times 3:2 (fifth). On C3, it's G4.

q: Which credentialed professionals use music to help patients reach health goals?
why: Music therapy is clinical work by credentialed music therapists, not just playing nice songs in a hospital.

q: Hearing loss caused by loud sounds has a name. What is it?
why: It can come from one very loud blast or from loud sound over time, and it is preventable.

q: Ringing in the ears with no outside sound, often after a loud concert, is called:
why: Tinnitus can ring, hiss, whistle or buzz. Loud noise is one common cause.

q: In a study in the journal Heart, fast music tended to do what to listeners' heart rate?
why: Tempo mattered more than taste: faster music raised heart rate and breathing, slow music calmed them.

q: True or false: science shows listening to Mozart makes you permanently smarter.
why: The 1993 study found a short boost on spatial tasks. Later reviews found little evidence of a special Mozart effect.

q: Gabby Giffords relearned to speak after a brain injury with help from which therapy?
why: She could sing words before she could say them. Her music therapist built speech from songs.

q: Live music therapy in the NICU is used to help which patients?
why: A 2013 study of 272 premature infants linked live music therapy to calmer vital signs and better feeding and sleep.

q: A steady beat can help people with Parkinson's disease do what better?
why: It's called rhythmic auditory stimulation. Steps lock onto the beat, and gait improves.

q: What does AMTA stand for?
why: AMTA is the national organization for music therapy in the United States.

q: The World Health Organization says hearing risk from loud listening depends on how loud it is and what else?
why: Volume times time is your sound dose. Same loudness, longer listening, more risk.

q: Musicians' earplugs are built to do what?
why: Flat attenuation keeps the balance of the music while turning everything down.

q: According to the NIDCD, long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above what level can cause hearing loss?
why: The louder the sound, the less time it takes to do damage. Sounds at or below 70 dBA are unlikely to cause harm.

q: The WHO-ITU safe listening standard sets an adult weekly sound allowance of:
why: Adults: 80 dB for 40 hours a week. The child mode is stricter: 75 dB for 40 hours.

q: Musician's focal dystonia usually shows up as what?
choices: Loss of control in a well-practiced movement
Sharp pain from a torn tendon
why: It's a task-specific movement disorder, usually without pain. It hits about 1 percent of musicians.

q: Melodic Intonation Therapy helps people with which condition?
why: Patients sing short phrases, then gradually drop the melody toward normal speech.

q: When music gives you chills, your brain releases which chemical linked to reward?
why: A 2011 Nature Neuroscience study measured dopamine release at peak musical pleasure.

q: Why might people with advanced Alzheimer's still recognize songs they've known a long time?
choices: Songs are kept in the spinal cord
Music is stored in the ears
Brain areas for long-known music are less damaged
why: A 2015 study in Brain found these regions showed less atrophy than the rest of the brain.

q: What does the MT-BC credential after a music therapist's name stand for?
why: It comes from the Certification Board for Music Therapists, which first gave the exam in 1985.

q: Johns Hopkins' Center for Music and Medicine pairs the medical school with which music conservatory?
why: The center launched in 2015 and studies music for Parkinson's, stroke, Alzheimer's and more.

q: In rhythmic auditory stimulation for Parkinson's, the cue tempo is usually set from what?
why: The metronome or music starts from the patient's own steps per minute, then guides it.

q: NIOSH recommends less than how much exposure per day at 100 dBA?
why: NIOSH allows 8 hours at 85 dBA and halves the time every 3 dB. Five halvings to 100 dBA gives 15 minutes.

q: Melodic Intonation Therapy was first described in 1973 at a VA hospital in which city?
why: Martin Albert, Robert Sparks and Nancy Helm developed it at the Boston VA.

q: Schlaug's 1995 study found a larger front corpus callosum in musicians who began training before what age?
why: The bridge between the brain's halves was larger in early starters. Whether training causes it is still debated.

q: Elbert's 1995 Science study found an enlarged brain map of which fingers in string players?
why: The fingering hand got more cortical real estate, especially in those who started young.

q: In Hyde and Schlaug's 2009 study, how long did children take weekly keyboard lessons before brain changes were seen?
why: About 15 months of weekly lessons in roughly 6-year-olds tracked with changes in motor and auditory areas.

q: In the 2011 musical-chills study, which brain region was more involved during anticipation of the peak?
why: The caudate ramped up before the chills; the nucleus accumbens took over at the peak.

q: A 2014 German study found professional musicians were about how many times likelier to get noise-induced hearing loss?
why: The adjusted hazard ratio was 3.61. The authors' fix: use the hearing protection that already exists.

q: The original 1993 'Mozart effect' study measured a short-term boost in what?
why: College students, spatial tasks, about 15 minutes of effect. A 2010 meta-analysis of about 40 studies found little left.

q: The American Music Therapy Association formed in 1998 by uniting which two groups?
why: The National Association for Music Therapy (1950) and the American Association for Music Therapy (1971) merged.

q: How many hours of clinical training does a music therapy degree require at minimum?
why: Fieldwork plus an internship adds to at least 1,200 hours before the board exam.

q: Who invented the piano?
why: Cristofori built it in Florence for the Medici court, with the earliest record from 1700.

q: The saxophone is named after its inventor. Who was he?
why: Adolphe Sax of Dinant, Belgium, patented the saxophone in 1846.

q: Which instrument do you play without touching it?
why: Your hands move near two antennas: one sets pitch, the other volume. Leon Theremin built it around 1920.

q: The trumpet belongs to which instrument family?
why: You buzz your lips into a cup mouthpiece. That buzz is what makes it brass.

q: How many strings does a violin have?
why: G, D, A, E, from low to high, tuned a 5th apart.

q: The ukulele was developed in which place?
why: Madeiran immigrants arrived in 1879 with the small machete, and Hawaii turned it into the ukulele.

q: The didgeridoo comes from which country?
why: Aboriginal players in northern Australia make it from eucalyptus trunks hollowed out by termites.

q: The steelpan was born in which country?
why: Players in the 1930s and 1940s hammered tuned notes into steel drums and later oil barrels.

q: Which instrument usually plays the A that the orchestra tunes to?
why: The oboe's pitch is hard to adjust and its tone cuts through, so everyone else matches it.

q: The sousaphone is named after which bandleader?
why: J. W. Pepper built the first one around 1893 to Sousa's specs, with the bell pointing straight up.

q: True or false: the saxophone is a woodwind, even though it's made of brass.
choices: True, but only the soprano sax
why: Family goes by how sound is made. The sax uses a single reed, so it's a woodwind.

q: Which of these woodwinds uses no reed at all?
why: The flutist blows across an edge, splitting the air stream. No reed required.

q: A B♭ clarinet reads a written C. What concert pitch comes out?
why: The B♭ clarinet sounds a major 2nd lower than written. Its name tells you what its C sounds like.

q: Which instrument plays the famous solo in Tchaikovsky's Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy?
why: Hammers strike metal plates for that music-box shimmer. The Nutcracker premiered in 1892.

q: How many pedals does a concert pedal harp have?
why: One pedal for each note name, and each pedal retunes that note in every octave.

q: Which American founding father invented the glass armonica?
why: In 1761 Franklin mounted glass bowls on a spinning rod. Mozart and Beethoven wrote for it.

q: The Hammond organ, introduced in 1935, makes its tone with what?
why: Each tonewheel spins next to a pickup and makes a near-pure tone. Drawbars mix them.

q: Antonio Stradivari made his famous violins in which Italian city?
why: Cremona was the violin-making capital, home to the Amati and Guarneri families too.

q: How many main slide positions does a trombone have?
why: Each position out lowers the pitch about a half step. First is all the way in, seventh all the way out.

q: In the Hornbostel-Sachs system, a drum with a stretched skin is called a:
why: The membrane vibrates. Bells and xylophones are idiophones because the whole body vibrates.

q: Cristofori's original name for the piano was gravicembalo col piano e ___.
why: Harpsichord with soft and loud. The name shrank to pianoforte, then just piano.

q: A horn in F reads a written C. What interval below it sounds?
why: Written C comes out as concert F, a perfect 5th down.

q: The E♭ alto saxophone sounds how far below its written pitch?
why: Written C sounds as the E♭ a major 6th below.

q: Which of these instruments sounds an octave higher than written?
why: The piccolo sounds an octave up. Guitar and double bass go the other way: an octave below written.

q: Guinness lists the world's largest musical instrument as a pipe organ in which U.S. city?
why: The Boardwalk Hall Auditorium Organ has about 33,000 pipes and holds the loudest-instrument record too.

q: On a theremin, one antenna controls pitch. What does the other control?
why: Hands never touch it. The antennas act like capacitor plates that sense your hands.

q: Who invented the celesta, in Paris in 1886?
why: Mustel replaced his father's tuning-fork design with metal plates. Tchaikovsky found it in Paris a few years later.

q: How many strings does a full-size concert pedal harp usually have?
why: 47 strings, seven per octave, about six and a half octaves.

q: Robert Moog's synthesizers set pitch using what standard?
why: Voltage-controlled oscillators: add a volt, go up an octave. That standard ran a generation of synths.

q: Roughly how many instruments by Antonio Stradivari survive today?
why: Most estimates land near 650, mostly violins, with about 50 cellos and a dozen violas.

q: Listen: two notes, one after the other. Octave or unison?
why: Same letter name, 12 half steps apart. C4 up to C5.

q: Listen to both notes. Is the second note higher or lower than the first?
why: C up to G. The second note climbs.

q: Listen to this chord. Major or minor?
why: C–E–G, C major. Bright, sunny, birthday-party energy.

q: Here's a different chord. Does it sound major or minor?
why: A–C–E, A minor. Lower the 3rd and the sun goes behind a cloud.

q: Count them. How many notes did you hear?
why: C, D, E, F, G: five notes walking up.

q: Two notes, back to back. What interval is it?
why: G and G again. Zero half steps apart, same exact pitch.

q: Listen again. Does the second note go up or down?
why: C5 down to C4. The second note drops an octave.

q: Which scale is this?
why: C to C on white keys: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.

q: How many clicks do you hear in this rhythm?
why: Four even beats, one full bar of 4/4.

q: Is this beat fast or slow?
why: 168 BPM is presto territory, nearly three beats a second. The tempo holds steady.

q: Name this melodic interval. It's the leap in 'Twinkle, Twinkle' on the second 'twinkle.'
why: C up to G, 7 half steps. The tune jumps exactly this far between its two 'twinkles.'

q: Two notes going up. What's the interval?
why: D up to F♯: 4 half steps, the bottom of a major chord.

q: Listen: low note, then a higher one. Which interval?
why: G3 up to C4, 5 half steps. 'Here Comes the Bride' opens with it.

q: Three notes stacked. Which chord quality?
why: B–D–F: two minor 3rds stacked. Tight and tense.

q: This chord sounds like a question mark. What is it?
why: C–E–G♯: two major 3rds. The raised 5th leaves it hanging.

q: Four notes this time. Which seventh chord is it?
why: G–B–D–F: a major triad plus a minor 7th. In C major that's V7, and it wants to go home to I.

q: Which scale or mode do you hear?
why: A to A on white keys. Counted from its parent key, C major, Aeolian is the mode on the 6th degree.

q: Two notes played together. Name the harmonic interval.
why: E and G at once, 3 half steps. The darker of the two 3rds.

q: A big leap up. Which interval is it?
why: C up to A, 9 half steps. 'My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean' opens with it.

q: A quick run. How many notes are in it?
why: C up to C, both ends counted: eight notes.

q: Seventh chord: half-diminished (ø7) or fully diminished (°7)?
why: B–D–F–A: diminished triad plus a minor 7th. It's the vii chord in C major, so ø7.

q: Same root, different top note. Is this one ø7 or °7?
why: B–D–F–A♭: three minor 3rds stacked. The top dropped a half step, so ø7 becomes °7.

q: Starting on F, is this scale Lydian or plain major (Ionian)?
why: F to F on white keys has B natural, a raised 4th. Lydian, with parent key C major.

q: Another scale on F. Listen to the 4th note. Lydian or major (Ionian)?
why: This one has B♭, the normal 4th. Plain F major.

q: Two notes at once. Tritone or perfect 5th?
why: C and F♯, 6 half steps. One half step short of the stable 5th, and it sounds like it.

q: Which seventh chord is this lush one?
why: C–E–G–B. The 7th sits a half step below the octave.

q: Name this seventh chord's quality.
why: D–F–A–C: minor triad plus a minor 7th. In C major that's ii7.

q: Starting on D, white keys only. Which mode is it?
why: D to D on white keys. Parent key C major, so its home chord is ii, never i.

q: Starting on G, white keys only. Which mode?
why: G to G with F natural: major with a lowered 7th. Parent key C major, home chord V.

q: Starting on E, white keys only. Name the mode.
why: E to F is a half step right away, and that low 2nd is Phrygian. Parent C major, home chord iii.

why: As of year-end 2025: "Luther" ran 13 weeks, the longest No. 1 for both Kendrick and SZA.

q: Which song gave Alex Warren his first Hot 100 No. 1 in 2025?
why: As of 2025: it reached No. 1 in its 16th week and stayed for 10 weeks in total.

q: Who was Spotify's most-streamed artist in the world in 2025?
why: As of Wrapped 2025: his fourth time on top, the first artist ever to do it four times.

q: Who won Video of the Year at the 2025 MTV VMAs?
why: As of September 2025: for "Brighter Days Ahead." Lady Gaga won Artist of the Year.

q: Which Harry Styles single debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 in early 2026?
why: As of 2026: the lead single from Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.

q: Which song won the Oscar for Best Original Song in March 2026?
why: As of March 2026: the first K-pop song to win an Oscar.

q: As of late 2026, whose song holds the record for most weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100?
why: As of November 2026: "Choosin' Texas" passed the 22 weeks of "All I Want for Christmas Is You."

q: The Life of a Showgirl's first week (about 4 million units) broke whose record?
why: As of October 2025: it passed 25's 3.48 million units from 2015.

q: At the 2026 Grammys, Kendrick Lamar passed whom to become the most-awarded rapper ever?
why: As of 2026: five wins that night took him past Jay-Z's 25.

q: Huntrix became the first girl group to top the Hot 100 since which group in 2001?
why: As of 2025: "Golden" ended a 24-year girl group drought at No. 1.

q: Which country won the Eurovision Song Contest in May 2026?
why: As of 2026: DARA won with "Bangaranga," Bulgaria's first ever win.

q: Kendrick Lamar's 2025 halftime show became the most-watched ever, passing whose 1993 show?
why: As of 2025: about 133.5 million viewers, just past Jackson's 133.4 million.

q: Which 2025 tour became the highest-grossing country tour in Billboard Boxscore history?
choices: Morgan Wallen's I'm the Problem Tour
Luke Combs' Growin' Up and Gettin' Old Tour
why: As of year-end 2025: about $407.6 million from just 32 shows.

q: Which 2025 tour became the highest-grossing co-headlining tour in history?
choices: Def Leppard and Mötley Crüe's Stadium Tour
Beyoncé and Jay-Z's On the Run II
Jay-Z and Kanye West's Watch the Throne Tour
Kendrick Lamar and SZA's Grand National Tour
why: As of year-end 2025: about $369.6 million from 42 shows, passing On the Run II.

q: Which act was named to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame class of 2026?
why: As of 2026: Iron Maiden joins Oasis, Wu-Tang Clan, Sade, Phil Collins and more.

q: Which Lady Gaga album won Best Pop Vocal Album at the February 2026 Grammys?
why: As of 2026: Mayhem (2025) took the pop album prize at the 68th Grammys.

q: Which composer kept writing music, including his Ninth Symphony, after losing most of his hearing?
why: Beethoven was profoundly deaf by the time the Ninth premiered in 1824. He heard it in his head, which is the best argument for ear training ever made.

q: Which child prodigy wrote his first little pieces at about age 5?
why: Mozart played the tunes and his dad wrote them down. He wrote his first symphony at about eight.

q: Who composed The Four Seasons?
why: Four violin concertos, one per season, published in 1725 with a poem for each. Program music before it had a name.

q: Who composed the music for the ballet The Nutcracker?
why: It premiered in St. Petersburg in December 1892 to mixed reviews, and now it sells out every December.

q: How many symphonies did Beethoven complete?
why: Nine, and the Ninth (1824) was his final complete symphony. 41 is Mozart's number, not his.

q: Which instrument did Chopin write almost all of his music for?
why: Every Chopin piece includes the piano, and most are for solo piano. No symphonies, no operas: he knew his lane.

q: Who wrote the famous Canon in D?
why: Johann Pachelbel wrote it for three violins and basso continuo over a two-bar bass line that repeats 28 times.

q: Mozart was born in Salzburg. Salzburg is in which country today?
why: Born January 27, 1756, in Salzburg, then its own archbishopric and now part of Austria.

q: In an opera, how do the performers tell most of the story?
why: Opera is a staged drama where the music runs the whole way through. If they mostly dance and never sing, you're at the ballet.

q: In a concerto, who stars out in front of the orchestra?
why: A concerto is built on a soloist and an orchestra trading ideas, competing and combining. The conductor just gets the cool stick.

q: In Prokofiev's Peter and the Wolf, which instrument plays the duck?
why: Bird is flute, duck is oboe, cat is clarinet, grandfather is bassoon, wolf is three horns. Every character gets its own sound.

q: Fanny Mendelssohn's younger brother was also a famous composer. What was his name?
why: Felix Mendelssohn. Six of Fanny's songs were published under his name because of how women composers were treated at the time.

q: Clara Schumann was one of the biggest concert stars of the 1800s on which instrument?
why: She debuted at nine, performed for about 60 years and was ranked alongside Liszt. Composer, pianist and the family breadwinner.

q: Which composer wrote Messiah, home of the Hallelujah chorus?
why: Handel's Messiah premiered in Dublin on April 13, 1742. The Hallelujah chorus closes Part Two.

q: Which composer is nicknamed the 'Father of the Symphony'?
why: Joseph Haydn helped lock in the Classical symphony and the string quartet. He's called father of both.

q: Odd one out: which composer is NOT from the Baroque period?
why: Baroque runs roughly 1600 to 1750. Chopin is a Romantic-era composer, born long after Bach, Handel and Vivaldi were gone.

q: Which came first? Whose birth was earliest?
why: Bach was born in 1685 and Mozart in 1756, a 71-year head start. Beethoven and Clara Schumann came after Mozart.

q: Beethoven's Fifth Symphony opens with which famous rhythm?
why: Da-da-da-DUM. The whole symphony is built on that one idea, and the 'fate knocking' story is legend, not proof.

q: Which instrument plays the famous slide that opens Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue?
why: Clarinetist Ross Gorman turned a written scale into a slide as a rehearsal joke, and Gershwin kept it. Sometimes the joke is the hook.

q: How many movements does a typical Classical-era symphony have?
why: Fast first movement, slow second, a minuet or scherzo third, fast finale. Four, with plenty of exceptions.

q: Hildegard of Bingen, abbess and one of the first composers known by name, lived in which century?
why: Hildegard lived from 1098 to 1179. Most plainchant is anonymous, so a named composer from then is rare.

q: Beethoven scratched whose name off the title page of his Third Symphony, the 'Eroica'?
why: When Napoleon crowned himself emperor, Beethoven scraped the name off so hard he tore a hole. Prince Lobkowitz got the dedication instead.

q: The 'K.' in Mozart catalogue numbers like K. 626 stands for whom?
why: Köchel published his chronological catalogue of Mozart's works in 1862. K. 626 is the Requiem.

q: Haydn's 'Surprise' Symphony, with its sudden loud chord, is which number?
why: Number 94 in G major: a quiet tune, then one loud chord. 45 is the 'Farewell', 101 the 'Clock', 104 the 'London'.

q: Who became the youngest winner of the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 2013, at age 30?
why: Caroline Shaw won for Partita for 8 Voices, written for Roomful of Teeth. An a cappella piece took the prize.

q: Which American composer wrote Short Ride in a Fast Machine and the opera Nixon in China?
why: Short Ride (1986) and Nixon in China (1987), his first opera, came out back to back.

q: Which composer wrote the 1976 opera Einstein on the Beach with director Robert Wilson?
why: No conventional plot, synthesizers instead of an orchestra, and a libretto of numbers and solfège syllables. It premiered at the Avignon Festival.

q: In 1933, which orchestra premiered Florence Price's Symphony in E minor, a first for an African American woman composer?
why: Frederick Stock conducted the Chicago Symphony in June 1933. Price had won first prize for the symphony in a composition contest.

q: Before she married Robert Schumann, what was Clara Schumann's last name?
why: Clara Wieck: her father, Friedrich Wieck, was her piano instructor and manager. Hensel was Fanny Mendelssohn's married name.

q: In which city did Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring cause an uproar at its 1913 premiere?
why: May 29, 1913, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées. How violent it got is still argued about, but the music won.

q: Who wrote the music and lyrics for Hamilton?
why: Miranda got the idea in 2008 reading Ron Chernow's biography on vacation. Best vacation reading in Broadway history.

q: Wicked tells the backstory of characters from which story?
why: Wicked follows Elphaba, the future Wicked Witch of the West, and her friendship with Glinda.

q: Who composed the music for The Phantom of the Opera musical?
why: Andrew Lloyd Webber. It opened in London's West End in October 1986 with Michael Crawford as the Phantom.

q: The Sound of Music was the last collaboration of which songwriting team?
why: Richard Rodgers wrote the music and Oscar Hammerstein II the lyrics. It opened on Broadway in 1959.

q: 'Hedwig's Theme' from Harry Potter is named after what kind of animal?
why: Hedwig is Harry's owl. John Williams' theme ended up meaning the whole wizarding world, not just the bird.

q: The Jaws shark theme builds fear by going back and forth between how many notes?
why: Two notes a half step apart, usually named E and F. Proof you don't need a lot of notes, just the right ones.

q: Which real-life singing family inspired The Sound of Music?
why: The musical came from Maria von Trapp's memoir. Rodgers and Hammerstein opened it on Broadway in 1959.

q: In The Phantom of the Opera, what does the Phantom wear to hide part of his face?
why: The first design was a full mask, but it was too hard to get off. The logo still shows the full one.

q: The Tony Awards honor the best work in what?
why: Named after Antoinette 'Tony' Perry, an actress and director. First handed out in 1947.

q: Who composed the music for Star Wars?
why: Williams won the Oscar for the 1977 Star Wars score. He has five competitive Oscars in all.

q: Who won the Oscar for the score of The Lion King (1994)?
why: Zimmer took Best Original Score. Elton John and Tim Rice won Best Song for 'Can You Feel the Love Tonight.'

q: Who composed the music for The Lord of the Rings film trilogy?
why: Howard Shore wrote the whole trilogy and won three Oscars for it.

q: Who wrote the music for Disney's Beauty and the Beast (1991)?
why: Alan Menken's music, Howard Ashman's lyrics. The title song and the score both won Oscars.

q: The musical Les Misérables is based on a novel by which author?
why: Victor Hugo's 1862 novel. Gaston Leroux wrote The Phantom of the Opera, in case that one tempted you.

q: Which show has the longest run in Broadway history?
why: Phantom closed April 16, 2023, after 13,981 performances. Chicago now holds the longest run still playing.

q: Who wrote the music for West Side Story?
why: Bernstein wrote the music; a young Stephen Sondheim wrote the lyrics. That was Sondheim's Broadway debut, in 1957.

q: What was Rodgers and Hammerstein's first musical together?
why: Oklahoma! opened on Broadway on March 31, 1943, and ran 2,212 performances on its first go.

q: Who wrote the music and lyrics for Wicked?
why: Stephen Schwartz wrote the songs; Winnie Holzman wrote the book. It opened on Broadway in 2003.

q: Which Sondheim musical mixes Cinderella, Jack, Little Red Riding Hood and Rapunzel?
choices: Sunday in the Park with George
why: Into the Woods (1987) ties four fairy tales to a new story about a Baker and his Wife. Every wish has a price.

q: Which came first on Broadway?
why: Phantom opened on Broadway in January 1988. The Lion King came in 1997, Wicked in 2003, Hamilton later still.

q: Which composer won Best Original Score Oscars for both Black Panther and Oppenheimer?
why: Göransson won for Black Panther and Oppenheimer, then a third in 2026 for Sinners.

q: Who became the first woman to win the Tony for Best Direction of a Musical, for The Lion King in 1998?
why: Julie Taymor also won the costume design Tony that night. The puppets alone deserve a trophy.

q: Hamilton is based on a biography by which historian?
why: Ron Chernow's 2004 book Alexander Hamilton. Chernow helped guide Miranda through the writing.

q: Hamilton set a record for Tony nominations in 2016. How many?
why: Sixteen nominations, eleven wins, including Best Musical. Eleven is the trap answer.

q: In what language was Les Misérables first written and staged in 1980?
why: Schönberg and Boublil's show began as a French concept album and a run at the Palais des Sports in Paris. London's English version came in 1985.

q: Ennio Morricone finally won a competitive Oscar in 2016 for which film?
choices: Once Upon a Time in the West
why: He'd already received an honorary Oscar in 2007. The Hateful Eight gave him his first competitive win at 87.

q: How many Oscars did Howard Shore win for The Lord of the Rings trilogy?
why: Best Score for Fellowship and Return of the King, plus Best Song for 'Into the West.'

q: Hans Zimmer won his second Oscar for which film?
why: Dune won at the 2022 Oscars, 27 years to the day after his Lion King win.

q: Which of these John Williams scores won the Oscar?
choices: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone
why: His five competitive wins: Fiddler on the Roof, Jaws, Star Wars, E.T. and Schindler's List.

q: Which show is the highest-grossing in Broadway history?
why: The Lion King passed Phantom's box office total in 2012 and kept going.

q: What instrument did Louis Armstrong play?
why: He started on cornet and moved to trumpet. Nicknames: Satchmo and Pops.

q: What is scat singing?
why: Scat swaps lyrics for syllables like 'doo-bee' so the voice can play like a horn.

q: What did B.B. King name his guitars?
why: He once ran back into a burning dance hall for his guitar. He named every guitar Lucille after that to remind himself not to do it again.

q: Which U.S. city is called the birthplace of jazz?
why: Congo Square in New Orleans is where rhythms that fed early jazz were played every Sunday.

q: Ella Fitzgerald is known by which nickname?
why: First Lady of Song. Lady Day was Billie Holiday, the Empress was Bessie Smith.

q: Which instrument did Duke Ellington play?
why: Ellington played piano and led his orchestra for 50 years. His real instrument was the whole band.

q: Odd one out: which jazz legend was NOT a trumpeter?
why: Charlie 'Bird' Parker played alto saxophone. The other three are trumpet royalty.

q: Which trumpeter made the album Kind of Blue?
why: Miles Davis, with John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley and Bill Evans. It's often called the best-selling jazz record ever.

q: Bessie Smith's nickname was what?
why: Her 1923 debut 'Downhearted Blues' made her a star. 'Mother of the Blues' was Ma Rainey.

q: What instrument did John Coltrane mainly play?
why: Coltrane played tenor sax, and later soprano too. He's on Kind of Blue.

q: What year was Miles Davis's Kind of Blue recorded?
why: Recorded in 1959. 'So What,' the opener, was cut on March 2.

q: Charlie Parker's group with which trumpeter got its style named 'bebop' in 1944?
why: Parker and Gillespie's small group played the Three Deuces in New York in late 1944, and the name 'bebop' stuck.

q: Who wrote the jazz ballad ''Round Midnight'?
why: Monk wrote it in the early 1940s. It's often called the most recorded jazz standard written by a jazz musician.

q: Which bluesman left the Mississippi Delta for Chicago in 1943 and switched to electric guitar?
why: Muddy Waters plugged in so he could be heard over noisy Chicago bars, and helped invent postwar Chicago blues.

q: Billie Holiday's nickname, given by saxophonist Lester Young, was what?
why: She called him 'Pres' and he called her 'Lady Day.' Best nickname trade in jazz.

q: Benny Goodman's 1935 show at the Palomar Ballroom is often called the spark of which era?
why: The Swing Era usually runs 1935 to 1946, when big bands were the pop music of America.

q: Who wrote 'Take the "A" Train,' the Duke Ellington Orchestra's theme song?
why: Billy Strayhorn wrote it in 1939, based on Ellington's subway directions to his house.

q: In Roman numerals, which three chords build a basic 12-bar blues?
why: I, IV and V, usually played as dominant 7ths. In C that's C7, F7 and G7.

q: Which Miles Davis recordings from 1949 and 1950 gave cool jazz its name?
why: A nine-piece band with tuba and French horn, arranged by Gerry Mulligan, Gil Evans and John Lewis. Calm, not sleepy.

q: Jazz fusion in the late 1960s mixed jazz mostly with what?
why: Fusion brought electric pianos, guitars and rock beats into jazz. Miles Davis led the charge.

q: What is Thelonious Monk's middle name?
why: Thelonious Sphere Monk, born in 1917 in Rocky Mount, North Carolina. Rarest middle name in jazz, maybe.

q: In 'So What,' how far does the bridge move the Dorian sound?
why: D Dorian for the A sections, E♭ Dorian for the bridge, then back. One half step, total lift.

q: In what year did John Coltrane's quartet record A Love Supreme?
why: One session, December 9, 1964, with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones. Four players, one statement.

q: Charlie Parker's 'Ko-Ko' is built on the chord changes of which standard?
why: New melody over the chords of Ray Noble's 'Cherokee,' recorded in 1945. Jazz calls that a contrafact.

q: John Coltrane's 'Giant Steps' cycles through three key centers spaced by what interval?
why: B, G and E♭ major, a major third apart. Their roots spell an augmented triad.

q: How many songs did Robert Johnson record in his whole career?
why: Twenty-nine songs in two sessions: San Antonio in 1936 and Dallas in 1937. Short catalogue, huge shadow.

q: Which 1926 Louis Armstrong Hot Five record made scat singing famous?
why: Recorded February 26, 1926. Not the first scat on record, but the one everybody copied.

q: In 1934, Ella Fitzgerald won Amateur Night at which Harlem theater?
why: November 21, 1934. She meant to dance, switched to singing, and won first prize.

q: What was Duke Ellington's birth name?
why: Edward Kennedy Ellington, born in Washington, D.C., in 1899. Mercer was his son.

q: Dizzy Gillespie's trademark trumpet had its bell bent upward at about what angle?
why: Someone fell on his horn at a 1953 party. He liked the sound and had trumpets built with a 45-degree bell.

q: The bodhrán frame drum is a big part of the traditional music of which country?
why: The bodhrán is an Irish frame drum, played with the hand or a small stick called a tipper.

q: What was the name of Bob Marley's band?
why: Bob Marley co-founded the Wailers with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer. It later became Bob Marley and the Wailers.

q: Bob Marley is the most famous star of which style?
why: Born in Nine Mile, Jamaica, in 1945. Reggae grew out of ska and rocksteady.

q: The Great Highland bagpipe comes from which country?
why: A bag, a chanter for the melody and three drones: two tenor, one bass. Loud enough to need no amp.

q: Mariachi music comes from which country?
why: Strings, voices and trumpets from western Mexico. UNESCO added mariachi to its heritage list in 2011.

q: Odd one out: three of these have strings. Which one is a drum?
why: The djembe is a goblet-shaped West African drum played with bare hands. The others get plucked.

q: The tango comes mainly from which country?
why: Tango grew up in Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s, so Uruguay gets credit too.

q: Samba is the famous sound of which country's Carnival?
why: Samba grew from Afro-Brazilian communities in Bahia and took off in Rio de Janeiro.

q: Ravi Shankar was a world-famous master of which instrument?
why: Ravi Shankar brought the sitar to audiences all over the world. Up to 13 extra strings under the frets ring along by themselves.

q: The sitar comes from which country?
why: The sitar has playing strings on top and extra strings underneath that ring by themselves.

q: Sitar master Ravi Shankar taught which Beatle?
why: Harrison studied sitar with Shankar in the mid-1960s and called him the 'Godfather of World Music.'

q: The tabla is played as a set of how many drums?
why: Two: the small dayan for the high, ringing tones and the big bayan for the bass.

q: The koto, a long plucked zither, is the national instrument of which country?
why: The koto is played with picks on three fingers. Movable bridges set the tuning.

q: How many strings does a Chinese erhu have?
why: Two strings and no fingerboard. Players press the strings in the air.

q: What was Celia Cruz's famous catchphrase?
why: 'Sugar!' It started in 1964 when a waiter asked if she wanted sugar in her coffee.

q: Nigerian star Fela Kuti created which style?
why: Afrobeat mixes highlife, funk, jazz and Yoruba music. Drummer Tony Allen counts as a co-founder.

q: The Buena Vista Social Club album brought back classic music from which country?
why: Recorded in Havana and released in 1997, it won a Grammy and became the best-selling world music album.

q: Gamelan, with its bronze gongs and metallophones, comes from which country?
why: Gamelan comes mainly from the islands of Java and Bali. It's a whole orchestra of bronze.

q: Flamenco comes from which region of Spain?
why: Song (cante), guitar (toque), dance (baile) and handclaps (palmas). UNESCO added it to its heritage list in 2010.

q: Which bossa nova song won the 1965 Grammy for Record of the Year?
why: Music by Antônio Carlos Jobim, sung by Astrud Gilberto with Stan Getz on sax.

q: How many strings does a standard Japanese koto have?
why: Thirteen, each with its own movable bridge. There's a 17-string bass koto too.

q: How many strings does the West African kora have?
why: Twenty-one strings over a big calabash gourd covered in cowhide. Griots, or jalis, play it.

q: The Andean charango's back was traditionally made from what?
why: Armadillo shell was traditional. Today it's made of wood, which protects the armadillos.

q: The bandoneón, heart of tango, is named after which German instrument dealer?
why: Heinrich Band sold it in Germany; sailors brought it to Argentina and Uruguay around 1870. Who actually invented it is still argued about.

q: On the Chinese erhu, where does the bow hair go?
choices: Over the top of the strings
why: The bow is threaded between the strings, so it never comes off the instrument.

q: Which instrument is considered the ancestor of the European lute?
why: The oud has a pear-shaped body and no frets. 'Lute' comes from the Arabic al-ʿūd, 'the wood.'

q: The polka started in the 1830s in which region?
why: Bohemia is now part of the Czech Republic. The name likely comes from the Czech půlka, 'half,' for the half-step.

q: Salsa took shape as a named style in which city during the 1960s and '70s?
why: Cuban and Puerto Rican musicians in New York built it from son and mambo, with Fania Records leading the way.

q: In what year did UNESCO add reggae music of Jamaica to its list of cultural heritage?
why: Added November 29, 2018. Reggae came out of ska and rocksteady in the late 1960s.

q: Through the 1970s, Fela Kuti led which band?
why: Koola Lobitos came first, Africa 70 ruled the 1970s, Egypt 80 came after. Positive Force is his son Femi's band.

q: Who invented the phonograph in 1877?
why: Edison recorded onto tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder. 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' was one of the first things he recorded.

q: What does a microphone do?
choices: Turns sound into an electrical signal
why: Mics turn sound into a signal; speakers do the reverse. Same idea, opposite direction.

q: In a mix, what does panning do?
choices: Moves a sound left or right
why: Panning places each sound somewhere between the left and right speakers. It's how the drummer can sound like they're on stage left.

q: What does reverb add to a sound?
choices: The sound of a room or space
why: Reverb is sound hanging in the air after it bounces off walls. Cathedral, closet, canyon: pick your room.

q: CD stands for what?
why: Sony and Philips developed it together, storing 16-bit digital audio.

q: The Beatles recorded nearly all their albums at which London studio?
why: Nearly everything from 1962 to 1970. The studio is named after the street, not the album.

q: Spotify was founded in which country?
why: Founded in Stockholm in 2006, it now streams music around the world.

q: In mixing, EQ is short for what?
why: EQ turns frequency bands up or down. The bass and treble knobs are the simplest EQ.

q: Which came first?
why: Order: CD, then MP3, then Auto-Tune, then Spotify. Formats stack up fast.

q: What's the main trick of the MP3 format?
choices: It makes audio files much smaller
why: MP3 drops sound details you're unlikely to hear, often cutting the file by 75 to 95 percent.

q: What does MIDI stand for?
why: MIDI lets keyboards, computers and drum machines talk to each other. A panel of music industry representatives agreed on it as the standard.

q: The Shure SM58, a live-vocal workhorse since 1966, is what type of microphone?
why: A cardioid dynamic mic: no phantom power needed, and built to survive a tour.

q: Guitarist Les Paul was a pioneer of which recording technique?
why: Les Paul layered part on top of part, one track at a time. He also helped invent the solid-body electric guitar.

q: Which producer is often called 'the fifth Beatle'?
why: George Martin produced the Beatles' records. He trained in classical music and played oboe.

q: Who produced Michael Jackson's album Thriller?
why: Thriller is the best-selling album of all time, around 70 million copies.

q: Rick Rubin co-founded which hip-hop label with Russell Simmons in 1984?
why: Rubin started Def Jam while he was still a student at NYU.

q: Who co-founded Spotify with Martin Lorentzon?
why: Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon founded it in 2006. It launched in 2008 in several European countries.

q: In mixing, what does a compressor do?
choices: Narrows the gap between loud and soft
why: A compressor turns loud parts down (and can bring quiet parts up) so the track sits more evenly.

q: Auto-Tune was developed in 1997 by which engineer?
why: Andy Hildebrand, a Ph.D. engineer, built it for Antares Audio Technologies. Cher's 'Believe' later turned it into an obvious effect.

q: DAW stands for what?
why: A DAW is the software you record, edit and mix in. Your whole studio, on one screen.

q: Which company built Les Paul's 8-track tape recorder, nicknamed 'The Octopus'?
why: Ampex built the eight-track deck for his home studio. He named it The Octopus.

q: Roland's Ikutaro Kakehashi shared a 2013 Technical Grammy for creating MIDI with whom?
why: Dave Smith of Sequential Circuits worked out the universal interface and named it MIDI.

q: The MP3 format was developed mainly by which German research organization?
why: Fraunhofer, led by Karlheinz Brandenburg, did most of the work. The .mp3 extension was picked in July 1995.

q: Dr. Dre co-founded Beats with which music executive?
why: Founded in 2006, first headphones in 2008, sold to Apple in 2014 for about $3 billion.

q: Which Swedish producer co-wrote and produced Britney Spears' '...Baby One More Time'?
why: Max Martin, born Karl Martin Sandberg, wrote and co-produced it in 1998, the first of a long run of hits.

q: Before it was renamed in 1976, Abbey Road Studios was known as what?
why: It opened in 1931 and took the Abbey Road name in 1976. The Beatles named their album after the street.

q: Pro Tools, the studio-standard DAW, was first developed by which company?
why: Digidesign launched Pro Tools in 1991. Avid bought Digidesign later, which is why the Avid answer looks so tempting.

q: The famous 'Amen break' drum loop, one of the most sampled ever, comes from a 1969 song by which group?
why: A seven-second drum break from 'Amen, Brother.' Hip-hop, then jungle, has borrowed it ever since.

q: Phantom power for condenser mics is standardly how many volts?
why: P48, 48 volts, sent down the mic cable. Dynamic mics don't need it.

q: Which Michael Jackson album was NOT produced by Quincy Jones?
why: Jones produced Off the Wall, Thriller and Bad. Bad (1987) was their last album together.
